claims.text: Selective chemical dealloying of a multicomponent precursor containing noble and less-noble metals can produce three-dimensional NM-HEA nanoframeworks.
The resulting NM-HEA nanoframeworks provide enhanced catalytic surface area.
Selective dealloying enables atomic-level control of NM-HEA nanoframeworks.
A homogeneous high-entropy precursor can contain noble metals such as Pt, Pd, and Au blended with less-noble metals.
Controlled acid etching preferentially dissolves the less-noble elements from the multicomponent precursor.
Dealloying can be conducted under acidic or electrochemical conditions.
Precise control of temperature, reagent concentration, and treatment time can prevent over-etching.
Selective dealloying forms an interconnected nanoporous framework composed predominantly of noble-metal atoms.
Removing less-noble atoms leaves behind a three-dimensional, high-surface-area nanostructure.
The nanostructure retains high-entropy mixing after selective removal of less-noble atoms.
Retained high-entropy mixing provides diverse and precisely controlled catalytic active sites.
Dealloyed NM-HEA nanoframeworks will have significantly greater catalytic surface area than the untreated homogeneous precursor.
Dealloyed NM-HEA nanoframeworks may have better catalytic activity than the untreated homogeneous precursor.
Overly aggressive dealloying conditions may collapse the framework.
Overly mild dealloying conditions may cause incomplete dealloying and limited nanostructuring.
SEM or TEM can be used to assess whether a three-dimensional nanoframework formed.
BET measurement can quantify changes in specific surface area after dealloying.

contradictions.description: The boundary explicitly predicts failure under conditions that are too aggressive or too mild, whereas the falsification rule says failure under any controlled dealloying condition falsifies the hypothesis. Thus, a single expected off-optimum failure would incorrectly falsify the broader claim that an appropriate dealloying window exists.

The hypothesis and mechanism state that dealloying offers precisely controlled active sites or atomic-level control, while the uncertainty field says the achievable degree of atomic-level control remains undetermined.
